title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC antecedent vs consequent judgment; Ps 119
pass_a_gloss: The cited examples are therefore off purpose: they treat judgment following the sin of those punished. Here the question is judgment anteeding the punished's sin. If GAR thought 'judgment of God' always means that in Scripture, he erred—Ps. 119:7, 12, 19, 29 take it otherwise. If he did not think so, why praise those places, and what force have they against Placeus?
pass_b_english: Therefore the examples brought forward are not to the purpose. For in those it is a matter of judgment following the sin of those on whom punishment is inflicted. Here the question is of a judgment anteeding the sin of those who are punished. Next, did the learned man think this is the perpetual signification of God's judgment in Scripture, or not? If he thought so, he erred: for not rarely it is taken otherwise, as is plain from Ps. 119:7, 12, 19, 29, &c. If he did not think so, to what end did he praise such places? and what force can they have to refute me?
source_text: Non sunt igitur ad propositum quae afferuntur exempla. In illis enim agitur de judicio sequente eorum, quibus poena irrogatur, peccatum. Hic vero quaestio est de judicio, antecedente eorum qui puniuntur, peccatum. Deinde censuitne vir doctus, hanc esse judicii Dei perpetuam in Scriptura significationem, necne? Si censuit, erravit: non raro enim aliter accipitur, ut patet ex Ps. 119. 7. 12. 19. 29. &c. Si non censuit, quorsum eiusmodi loca laudavit? & quam vim habere possunt ad me refellendum?

choices.choice: Cited examples are consequent; Ps 119 shows other senses

bible_refs.note: judgment of God taken otherwise than vindicative
